title: The show home rule

beats.say: Would you hand a stranger the keys to your house just to fix a leaky tap?
An AI coding agent is a helper that reads your files and runs commands for you. What it reads is sent off your machine to be processed. So whatever it sees, it has really seen.
The safe way is a show home. Build a copy that looks real, with the same rooms and the same awkward doors, but nobody's real belongings inside. Keep the real house locked.
Four habits do this. Use no real data. Lock the real folders. Fake the sample. And ask for counts, not customer lists.

check.q: What is the point of the show home in the analogy?
opts: It lets the helper work on something realistic without real customer belongings
It makes the helper work faster
It hides the helper from your laptop
check.why: The sample keeps the real shape and awkward cases so the work is useful, while the real customer data stays locked away.

work: Ask your team where a sample of your data lives that has no real customers in it.
Before using an AI helper on a task, say which folder it is allowed to see.

title: Four controls, step by step

beats.say: How do you give an agent data to debug without giving it a single real customer?

First, the agent works on dev or sample data and holds no production credentials. Then add deny rules in settings: deny Read of data slash raw, and Read of exports. Now even if it tries, the read is refused.

Next, build a masked sample. Hash emails with a secret key, swap names for fake ones, shift dates by a fixed number of days, bucket amounts. Sample one thousand rows from ten million. Keep the nulls, duplicates and decimal commas, because those are the bugs.
Finally, watch what comes back. Query results flow into the agent's context. Ask for count nulls per column, not show rows with null email.

check.q: Which request is safest to give an agent?
opts: Show rows where email is null
Count nulls per column
Print the first 50 rows of the raw export
check.why: Results come back into the agent's context. A count reveals no identities, while rows do.

work: Add deny rules for your raw data and exports folders in the agent settings.
Write a script that makes a 1,000 row masked sample and keeps the odd cases.
Remove production credentials from any environment where an agent runs.

title: Why hashing is not anonymising

beats.say: You hashed every email, so the data is anonymous, right? Not quite.
A plain hash is predictable. The same email always gives the same output. An attacker hashes a list of common emails and matches them against yours. That guessing attack works.
So use HMAC, a keyed hash, with a secret salt kept out of the repo. Without the key, guessing fails. Even so, treat the result as personal data.

show.title: Keyed hash
show.note: Key stays out of the repo and out of the agent's reach

beats.say: Other traps: free text and long strings can hide names. Logs and query output bring real values back into context. And a count of one is still one person.

show.title: Gotchas
items: A group of one is one person
Keyed hash is still personal data

check.q: Why is a plain unkeyed hash of emails weak protection?
opts: Hashes are too long to store
The same email always gives the same hash, so common emails can be guessed
Hashes cannot be joined across tables
check.why: Determinism lets attackers hash likely emails and match them. A secret key in HMAC stops that, but the data is still personal.

work: Replace plain hashes with HMAC and store the key in a secret manager.
Scan free text columns for names and emails before sharing a sample.
Check agent logs for pasted rows.

title: Fences, cost and when to choose differently

beats.say: Deny rules are good, so why are they not enough?

show.text: Why is a fence not enough?

beats.say: Because a deny rule is a fence on one laptop. A new teammate, a new tool, or a typo in a path, and the fence is gone. The strong control is upstream: the agent never gets production credentials at all.
So build masked sample generation into the pipeline. Refresh it weekly, review it, and test that edge cases survive. The cost is upkeep. Samples drift, and stale ones stop reproducing real bugs.

Choose synthetic data for lowest risk, masked data for realistic quirks. If a bug only shows at production scale, do not loosen the fence. Have a cleared human debug it, and hand the agent only the aggregates.

check.q: A bug only reproduces on full production data. What is the best move?
opts: Give the agent read access to production for one day
Have a cleared human debug it and share only aggregates with the agent
Hash the whole table and share it
check.why: Loosening the fence breaks the guarantee. A cleared person works on real data, and the agent sees only safe aggregates.

work: Automate masked sample refresh and review it like code.
Decide a written rule for who may debug on production data.
Test that nulls, duplicates and decimal commas survive every refresh.

title: The consultant on the phone

beats.say: Does your code leave your laptop when an AI assistant helps you? Not quite. But what it reads does.

show.text: Your code stays. What it reads travels.
show.sub: A question about AI assistants and privacy

beats.say: Picture a consultant on a phone call. Your filing cabinet stays in your office. But every page you read aloud, they hear, and their company may keep a record.

chip.text: The cabinet stays; the pages read out do not

beats.say: In Claude Code, anything that becomes context is read aloud like that. Your prompts, files it opens, command results, pasted logs and screenshots.
So a query that shows one hundred customers reads their names and emails down the phone. Keep those pages in the cabinet.

chip.text: Names and emails should not be read out

check.q: In the consultant analogy, what does the filing cabinet stand for?
opts: Everything Claude reads and sends as context
Your code and data that stay on disk unless read into context
The transcript saved by the provider
The model's training data
check.why: The cabinet is the data sitting on your machine. It only leaves when its contents are read aloud, meaning they become context.

work: List what you have pasted or let an assistant read this week, and ask yourself if any of it was customer data.
Describe the rule to a teammate in one line: what Claude reads is what gets sent.

title: What gets sent on each turn

beats.say: You type one prompt. What exactly gets sent to the model?
Everything that becomes context goes to the provider, so it can write the next reply. That means your prompt, files Claude reads, command outputs, pasted logs and screenshots.

chip.text: Only what is read becomes context

beats.say: Say Claude runs select star from customers limit one hundred. Those hundred rows come back as output. They join the context and travel with the request. Your database stayed put, but the rows it printed did not.

chip.text: Printed rows leave, the database does not

beats.say: Locally, the transcript is saved too, under dot claude slash projects. So a second copy sits on your own disk.

chip.text: Pasted data also lives on your disk

check.q: Claude runs a query and the output shows 100 customer rows. What has happened?
opts: Nothing leaves, since the database is on your machine
The rows are now in context and are sent to the provider
Only the SQL text is sent, not the rows
The rows are sent only if you approve a second prompt
check.why: Command output becomes context, and context is sent to generate the next reply. The database stays put, but the printed rows travel.

work: Before letting an assistant run queries, check whether the output would contain real customer fields.
Find your transcript folder and look at what a past session saved.

title: Gone is not gone

beats.say: You pasted a production log by mistake. Can you take it back?

show.sub: Pasted a production log by mistake

beats.say: Not really. Once the text is in context, it has already gone to the provider, and it stays in the conversation, so later turns carry it along too.
How long the provider keeps it, and whether it may train on it, depends on your account type and settings. Consumer plans have a training privacy setting. Commercial terms differ.
And the local transcript keeps whatever was pasted, on disk. Names, emails and secrets all sit there until you remove them.

chip.text: Delete it yourself, it will not vanish

beats.say: Interviewers probe this: a head of a production extract can be enough to breach GDPR, India's DPDP, or a customer contract.

chip.text: A small sample can still be a breach

check.q: You paste a log with customer emails into a session, then notice and delete your message. What is the safest assumption?
opts: It never left your machine because you deleted it
It was probably sent as context and may also be in the local transcript
Only the provider's copy exists, not a local one
It is safe if you are on a commercial plan
check.why: Context is sent to generate replies, and transcripts are saved locally. Retention and training depend on your plan, so treat the data as already exposed.

work: Write a short rule for what to do when sensitive data is pasted: report it, review the plan's terms, clear the local transcript.
Never run head or select star on production extracts inside an AI session.

title: Designing so nothing sensitive can leak

beats.say: How do you let a team use AI on data work without leaking customers? Don't rely on people being careful.
Control what can be read. Give development access to masked views or synthetic fixtures, and keep raw production tables out of reach. Whatever Claude can read can leave.

chip.text: What it cannot read, it cannot send

beats.say: The trade-off is cost. Masking pipelines take effort, and fake data hides some real bugs. So inspect schemas and aggregates first, and sample real rows only in an approved environment.

show.title: Trade-offs
items: Synthetic data can hide real bugs
Real rows only in approved environments

beats.say: Then settle the paperwork. Check which plan your company uses, what its retention and training terms say, and whether your contracts allow it. If not, don't use the tool on that code.

check.q: Which control best reduces leak risk for AI use on data pipelines?
opts: Ask engineers to avoid pasting customer data
Give the session access only to masked or synthetic data
Delete transcripts every Friday
Switch to a longer context window
check.why: Anything readable can become context and leave. Restricting access to masked or synthetic data removes the risk structurally instead of relying on people.

work: Build a masked view or synthetic fixture set for the tables engineers most often inspect.
Ask your employer which plan and data terms apply to AI tools, and write down which repositories are allowed.

title: House rules for a note-taking helper

beats.say: Imagine you hire a helpful contractor who keeps notes on everything you tell them. Who else could read those notes?
Settings are like house rules. Shred old notes after a set number of days. Stop sending optional reports back to head office. Or make the helper work only through your own company front desk.

show.title: Three house rules
items: Shred old notes after some days
Skip optional reports to head office
Work only via your company front desk

beats.say: But a rule about shredding does not undo what you already said out loud. So never hand over customer secrets just because the rules are tight.

show.text: Rules shrink the footprint. They don't make secrets safe to share.

check.q: In the analogy, why can't house rules make it safe to tell the helper customer secrets?
opts: Rules only work on weekends
The helper already heard what you said
Shredding is always illegal
check.why: The rules limit leftovers and extra reporting, but anything you already shared has been heard. The safe move is not sharing secrets at all.

work: List what kind of customer data you handle that must never be pasted into an AI tool.
Ask your team which house rules, like retention and telemetry, are already switched on.

title: Three settings and what they actually do

beats.say: Where does your conversation go after you close the terminal?

Claude Code saves transcripts on your own disk. The setting cleanupPeriodDays decides how many days they stay. Set it to seven, and older files get deleted. Shorter means less history sitting around for someone to find.

Two environment variables cut optional traffic. Set DISABLE underscore TELEMETRY to one, or CLAUDE underscore CODE underscore DISABLE underscore NONESSENTIAL underscore TRAFFIC to one. Usage stats and similar extras stop. Your prompts still go to the model, or nothing would work.
In companies, requests can go through a gateway, or Amazon Bedrock, or Google Vertex. Then data is covered by agreements your company already signed.

check.q: You set DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1. What still reaches the model?
opts: Nothing, everything is blocked
Your prompts and the files Claude reads
Only usage statistics
check.why: Telemetry flags only stop optional extras. Prompts and context must still be sent for the model to answer.

work: Set cleanupPeriodDays to a short value that suits your team.
Add the telemetry variables to your shell or managed config and verify they are active.

title: Why telemetry off is not data safe

beats.say: You turned telemetry off. So is your data safe to paste? No.

show.text: Telemetry off is not data safe
show.sub: It only trims the side channel

beats.say: Telemetry is only the optional side channel. The prompt itself, plus any file contents or tool output Claude reads, still travels to the model to get an answer. That is essential traffic, so those switches never touch it.
Cleanup only affects the local copy. A transcript may hold pasted secrets in plain text until it expires, and deleting it later does not recall what was already sent.

show.title: Cleanup limits
items: Only the local copy is removed
Secrets sit in plain text until expiry
Deleting does not recall sent data

beats.say: A gateway changes who holds the data and under what contract. It does not redact anything. Keep customer data out at the source: use masked samples and synthetic rows.

show.text: Mask it before it gets near the prompt

check.q: A team routes through Bedrock and disables telemetry. What is true?
opts: Pasting raw customer data is now fine
Customer data should still be masked first
Transcripts no longer exist locally
check.why: Routing changes agreements and who holds the data. It does not redact content, and local transcripts still exist until cleanup.

work: Check a recent transcript on disk for pasted secrets or customer values.
Create a masked or synthetic sample dataset for prompts and debugging.

title: Settings are the last layer, not the plan

beats.say: You are designing privacy for a hundred engineers using an AI coding tool. Are settings enough?
No. Settings are the last layer. Any single flag can be missed or reverted, so push them through centrally managed company configuration, not hope.

show.title: Settings alone are fragile
items: Flags can be missed or undone
Treat them as defence in depth

beats.say: Routing through Bedrock or Vertex buys contract terms, regional control and audit logs. It costs setup, and you own the gateway uptime. Choose it when regulators or customers demand it. A small team with no regulated data may not need it.

The stronger control is upstream. Give engineers masked or synthetic datasets, and restrict production access, so customer data never reaches the laptop. Then shorter retention and less telemetry are just extra defence.

check.q: Which control gives the strongest protection for customer data?
opts: Shorter cleanupPeriodDays
Disabling telemetry
Keeping raw data off laptops with masked datasets and restricted access
check.why: Upstream controls stop the data from ever being exposed. Retention, telemetry and routing only reduce the footprint afterward.

work: Propose masked or synthetic datasets as the default for dev and AI-assisted work.
Decide with security whether a gateway or cloud provider route is needed, based on regulation and cost.

title: The whiteboard in the kitchen

beats.say: Imagine a café where the cook writes each customer's phone number on a whiteboard in the kitchen. Why would anyone do that?
Nobody means to. A busy cook jots it down to fix one order, and then it stays there for months. Software does the same. Personal data, called PII, slips into places that never needed it.

show.title: How it happens
items: A quick note to fix one problem
PII means details that identify a person

beats.say: Here is the good news. You can hire a proofreader to read the blueprints of your kitchen, meaning your code, without ever meeting a customer. It flags every whiteboard, every photocopy, every forgotten note.
Your job is to ask, then decide what to remove.

check.q: In the café story, what does the AI proofreader read?
opts: The blueprints, meaning the code
The customers' phone numbers
The kitchen's daily sales
check.why: The agent reviews code, which is safe to share. Real customer data stays on your side.

work: Pick one repo and ask an agent to list places where personal data might be written down unnecessarily.
Share only code with the agent, never real customer rows.
Pick the worst finding and remove it this week.

title: Four leaks an agent can spot

beats.say: How can an AI find a privacy leak without ever seeing a customer's data?

show.sub: The leak is visible in the code

beats.say: It reads code. It searches for log calls and print statements that include fields like email or phone. One debug line printing a whole request can write ten thousand emails a day into log files that dozens of engineers can read.
Next it follows each field. If the warehouse stores emails only to count orders, a hashed id or a plain count does the job, and the raw email can go.
Then it checks the lifecycle. Is there a delete path for each store, and is retention enforced, say at ninety days? Finally it scans test fixtures for real names copied from production.

show.title: Lifecycle and tests
items: Retention actually enforced, for example 90 days
No production names in test fixtures

beats.say: Ask for file and line, ranked by risk.

show.title: The prompt
show.text: Review this repo for places where personal data is logged, stored without need, or copied into tests. File:line, ranked.

check.q: The warehouse stores emails only to count orders. What is the best fix?
opts: Encrypt the email column and keep it
Store a hashed id or a count instead
Move the emails to a log file
check.why: If the job is counting, raw emails are not needed. Data you never store cannot leak.

work: Search your logging calls for fields like email, phone and address.
List which tables hold personal data and what each one is used for.
Ask the agent for a ranked file and line report and triage the top five.

title: When a clean report is not clean

beats.say: Your AI review says the repo is clean. Can you trust that?

show.sub: Absence of findings is not proof

beats.say: Not fully. The agent sees code, so it can miss what happens at runtime. A logger that prints a whole object, or an error handler that dumps the request body, hides PII behind a name like payload.

Deletion is trickier. Deleting the user row is not erasure if copies live in the warehouse, a search index, caches and backups. A soft delete flag only hides the row. And a ninety day retention setting means nothing without a job that runs it.

show.title: Erasure gotchas
items: Copies in warehouse, search, caches, backups
Soft delete only hides the row
Retention setting needs a job that runs

beats.say: So treat findings as leads. Verify each in a safe test environment with fake data, never by pasting real customer records into the chat.

check.q: A user row is deleted with a soft delete flag. Is the person's data erased?
opts: Yes, the row is gone
No, the data still exists and copies may live elsewhere
Yes, if retention is set to 90 days
check.why: A soft delete only hides the row. True erasure must reach the data itself and every copy.

work: Trace one user's data through every store and mark which copies a delete would miss.
Check that each retention setting has a scheduled job behind it.
Reproduce each finding using synthetic data, not real records.

title: Review is not a control

beats.say: Should an AI review be your privacy control?
No. It is a great detector but a weak guarantee. Run it twice and it may rank things differently, and an auditor wants evidence that repeats.

Use it to discover patterns, then turn each into a hard rule. Redact fields in the logging layer itself. Tag personal columns in the schema so a CI check fails when one appears in a new table. Generate synthetic fixtures instead of copying production.
Cost is small. One pass over a large repo takes minutes and a few dollars, but split a monorepo by service so findings keep their file and line.

show.title: Cost and scale
items: Minutes and a few dollars per pass
Keep file and line in every finding

beats.say: Spend the savings on the expensive part: a tested erasure pipeline across every copy.

show.sub: Every copy, not just the main table

check.q: What is the best way to use a useful AI privacy finding long term?
opts: Re-run the AI review before each audit
Turn it into an automated rule such as log redaction or a CI check
Add a note to the wiki
check.why: Automated rules are deterministic and repeatable. The AI discovers patterns and the rules enforce them.

work: Add redaction to your shared logging layer so PII fields are masked by default.
Tag personal columns in the schema and fail CI when one appears in a new table.
Replace production-copied fixtures with generated synthetic data.
